title: Survival forests associate clinical and treatment-plan features with glioma survival
summary: A retrospective 95-patient high-grade glioma study used random survival forests to relate clinical characteristics and radiotherapy dose-volume features to observed survival. Age, tumor volume, grade, performance status, IDH status and a dose-coverage feature were selected by the learned model. This is an exploratory cohort association; the study does not establish that changing radiation dose improves survival or that its prediction performance generalizes to new hospitals.

evidence.tested: The source analyzes 95 historical patients, randomly dividing 57 for model development and 38 for testing. The survival forest selects clinical factors and a treatment-plan dose-coverage feature associated with recorded outcomes.
evidence.unknown: Continuous variables were converted using outcome-optimized cut points before the described split; preprocessing isolation is not established, so reported test accuracy may be optimistic. Feature selection and small-cohort risk thresholds need validation. Treatment choices, tumor size and case mix can confound dose–survival relationships. Decision-curve analysis is model-based, not demonstrated clinical utility, and no causal dose-prescription guidance follows.
evidence.ai_role: The survival forest learns nonlinear relationships between clinical/dose-volume features and survival, selecting a multifeature risk representation for retrospective outcome analysis.
